title: "Lab 10: Relational And Typed Data"
execute:
  enabled: false
---

## Goal

Clean strings, categories, and timestamps; join the supplied service-event log
to the building registry; and prove that every event remains exactly once.

## Setup

Create:

```text
week10/
  week10-clean-types.R
  week10-join-audit.R
  data/
    week10-building-registry.csv
    week10-service-events.csv
```

Download:

- [week10-building-registry.csv](../data/week10-building-registry.csv)
- [week10-service-events.csv](../data/week10-service-events.csv)
- [week10-clean-types.R](../code/r/week10-clean-types.R)
- [week10-join-audit.R](../code/r/week10-join-audit.R)

The tables contain invented teaching data.

## Part A: Write The Data Contract

Before coding, record each table's row meaning, key, expected row count, and
intended relationship. Identify which table defines the observations that must
remain after joining.

## Part B: Inspect Raw Strings

Count raw building keys, issue labels, and severity labels. Annotate the
differences you believe are superficial. State each proposed normalization
rule before applying it.

## Part C: Clean And Validate Text

Run `week10-clean-types.R`. Verify cleaned key syntax and the exact issue set.
Add a table showing raw and cleaned values side by side.

Explain why syntactically valid `BLDG-99` still requires a registry check.

## Part D: Build The Severity Factor

Confirm the factor order is low, medium, high. Deliberately introduce an
unexpected severity label and show how the missing-value check exposes it.
Restore the original data afterward.

## Part E: Parse Date-Times

Parse the full timestamp with the declared time zone, then derive date, hour,
and month. Check all timestamps parsed and retain the full timestamp.

Explain what information would be lost by replacing it with `as.Date` alone.

## Part F: Check Keys Before Joining

Confirm `building_id` is unique in the registry and `event_id` is unique in the
event log. State what row multiplication a duplicated registry key could cause.

## Part G: Audit Unmatched Rows

Use `anti_join` in both directions. Record the unknown event key and the
registered building without an event. Give a plausible investigation step for
each without declaring either row wrong automatically.

## Part H: Join And Verify

Run the declared many-to-one left join. Verify row count, event-key uniqueness,
matched and unmatched counts, and response-hour preservation.

Create a zone summary that retains the unknown event under an `unmatched`
label. Confirm its counts sum to nine.

## Deliverable

Submit:

- one runnable `.R` script;
- raw-to-clean value comparisons;
- factor and timestamp checks;
- both unmatched-row tables;
- the joined event table and post-join contract;
- the zone summary;
- a short note explaining why the chosen join preserves the event population.

## AI Use

If you use an LLM, record its proposed row meanings, keys, relationship, join
type, and cleaning rules. Verify all of these independently before accepting
its code.
